prompt: Brightquay Software will launch VaultLatch in the EU in 2028. It's a commercial password manager, sold as a desktop app and browser extension. We expect customers to use it for about seven years. Assume that at launch we won't have applied any harmonised standards, common specifications or EU cybersecurity certification scheme. The product team's plan: self-assess under internal control (module A), offer three years of support, and leave the end-of-support date for the website FAQ later on. What's wrong with the plan under the CRA?

This is the privacy notice for a small online retailer, shown when customers give us their data at checkout. Please check it against Article 13 GDPR and give me only the genuine gaps, with the provision for each and suggested wording. I don't want false alarms: flag it if something looks like a gap but isn't.

documents.name: pellwick-privacy-notice.txt
documents.content:
PELLWICK CYCLES PRIVACY NOTICE

Who we are. Pellwick Cycles Oy of Helsinki, a 12-person online retailer of bicycle parts, is the controller. Contact us at privacy@pellwick.example. We have not appointed a data protection officer.

What we collect and why. We use your name, address, email and payment details to fulfil your order (legal basis: performance of a contract). We keep invoices to meet accounting law (legal basis: legal obligation). We screen orders for fraud (legal basis: legitimate interests, namely preventing payment fraud against us and our customers). We send our monthly newsletter if you tick the box at checkout (legal basis: consent).

Who receives your data. We share your data with payment processors, couriers and IT hosting providers.

International transfers. Our order database is hosted by a provider in the United States, so your data is transferred there.

How long we keep your data. We keep your data for as long as we need it.

Your rights. You may request access to your data, and rectification, erasure or restriction of processing. You may object to processing and you have a right to data portability. Write to privacy@pellwick.example.

Do you have to give us your data? We need your name, address and payment details to complete an order. Without them we cannot deliver. The newsletter is optional.

Automated decisions. We do not make decisions based solely on automated processing.

prompt: Quillmere Digital Assets is an authorised EU crypto-asset service provider with 8 staff and annual turnover of EUR 1.5 million. It is not a trading venue. The founder believes that as a tiny firm it can use the Article 16 simplified ICT risk management framework and has no duties on testing, third-party strategy or the register of information. Please set out what actually applies under DORA on: (1) Article 16, (2) resilience testing, including TLPT, (3) the ICT third-party risk strategy and the register of information.

I am the only security person at Pellmoor Analytics, 35 staff. I wrote most of our security policies and I run the access management and vendor review processes. We need an internal audit before our ISO 27001 stage audit and my managing director says I should just do it myself, since nobody else understands this stuff and we have no budget. How do I do this credibly?

Today is 31 October 2026. Marrowgate Media is a provider of three AI systems in the EU: (A) an image generator on the market since February 2026; (B) a synthetic voice generator first placed on the market on 14 September 2026; and (C) a customer-support chatbot on the market since 2025, used by the public. Our counsel says the AI Omnibus pushed all Article 50 transparency duties to December 2027, so nothing is needed yet. For each product, tell me which Article 50 duty applies and the date it applies from.

Our patching policy at Corvane Health Software says critical vulnerabilities are patched within 7 days. Reality from the last two quarters is a median of about 30 days, because each patch goes through full regression. We are preparing for an ISO 27001 audit in six weeks. The head of engineering wants to change the policy to 30 days this week and keep the document's original approval date so it looks settled. What would you do?

I handle vendor risk at Solwick Payroll. We run on a major managed database provider and we are preparing for our own SOC 2. I downloaded the provider's latest assurance report and filed it. My manager asked, 'Good, so the database side is covered for us, right?' The report ends in March and it is now late October. It has a section listing things customers are expected to do, and I have not read that part. What do I tell her, and what should I actually do with the report?

Our board memo on the AI Act goes out on Monday. Assume today is 31 October 2026 and that Harbourlight built the driver scoring tool itself. Check it against the AI Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. List each statement that is legally wrong, with the correct position and the provision. Do not flag anything that is correct.

documents.name: ai-act-board-memo.txt
documents.content:
HARBOURLIGHT FREIGHT: AI ACT POSITION MEMO FOR THE BOARD
Position as of 31 October 2026, reflecting Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

1. Prohibited practices. Article 5 has applied since 2 February 2025. Breach of a prohibition carries a fine of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher.

2. AI literacy. Article 4 requires us to take measures to support the development of AI literacy of staff who operate AI on our behalf. It does not require us to guarantee any specific level of literacy for any individual. Our annual training module meets this approach.

3. Chatbot disclosure. Our shipment-tracking chatbot, which we built and put into service in 2025, has had to tell users they are talking to an AI system since 2 August 2026. The Omnibus did not defer this, so the disclosure banner stays live.

4. High-risk systems. Our driver performance-scoring tool is high-risk under Annex III. The high-risk requirements in Chapter III, Sections 1 to 3, applied from 2 August 2026, so we are already late and must finish the conformity work this quarter.

5. Product-embedded AI. AI classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) and Annex I has until 2 August 2028.

6. Bias testing. For our driver scoring tool, we rely on Article 10(5) of the AI Act as the legal basis for processing special category data in bias testing.

7. Logs. Once the high-risk rules apply, as deployer we must keep automatically generated logs under our control for at least six months, unless other law provides otherwise.

8. General-purpose models. Chapter V obligations for providers have applied since 2 August 2025. We do not provide any such model.

prompt: Under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772, when do recurring ICT-related incidents that are individually not major count together as one major incident, and how often must a financial entity check for this? Assume it is not a microenterprise or an Article 16(1) entity.

Compliance lead at Kestrelmoor Clinics here. We committed to quarterly access reviews on the patient scheduling system for our ISO 27001 programme, and the last two quarters simply did not happen because the IT manager was on long-term leave. Our audit is next month. A colleague suggests running a review this week and dating the records to June and September so there is no gap. How should I handle this?

Engineering lead at Marrowbank Data. At 2am last Tuesday, during a customer outage, one of our seniors pushed a hotfix straight to production using an admin bypass of branch protection, with no reviewer. It fixed the outage. We are mid-way through our SOC 2 observation period and our change process says every change needs a peer review. Someone suggests opening a backdated pull request with an approval. How should this be handled, and should we change anything?

Corvane Assurance, an EU insurance undertaking that is not a microenterprise, plans to sign the attached extract with a provider of its policy administration platform. The platform supports a critical function. Corvane has been told by its competent authority that it is identified for TLPT. Review the extract against Article 30 of DORA. List each clause that is non-compliant, why, and the fix. Do not list clauses that are fine. Comment only on the clauses shown.

documents.name: Master Services Agreement extract, Corvane and Provider
documents.content:
MASTER SERVICES AGREEMENT: EXTRACT

1. Services. Provider delivers the policy administration platform described in Schedule 1. Subcontracting of any part of the platform is permitted only on the conditions set out in Schedule 4.

2. Service levels. Schedule 2 sets precise quantitative and qualitative performance targets, including 99.95% monthly availability, and the corrective actions that apply when a target is missed.

3. Locations. Services are currently provided from Spain and data is stored in Ireland. Provider may move the provision of the services or the storage of data to any other country at its discretion, and has no duty to tell the Customer.

4. Data. Provider protects the availability, authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data, including personal data. On termination or Provider's insolvency, Provider gives the Customer access to its data and returns it in an easily accessible format.

5. Incident assistance. Provider gives assistance on any ICT incident relating to the services. This assistance is charged at the day rates fixed in Schedule 5 of this Agreement.

6. Audit. The Customer's sole audit right is to receive Provider's annual independent assurance report. Neither the Customer, any third party it appoints, nor any regulator may access or inspect Provider's premises or systems.

7. Testing. Provider tests its business contingency plans each year. Provider does not take part in customers' threat-led penetration tests.

8. Exit. On termination for any reason, Provider continues the services for a mandatory transition period of 18 months, so that the Customer can migrate to another provider or in-house.

9. Termination. Either party may terminate on 12 months' written notice. The Customer may terminate immediately for material breach.

10. Cooperation. Provider fully cooperates with the Customer's competent and resolution authorities.

prompt: Quillmere Software runs a purely browser-based HR SaaS. There is no installable client, mobile app, on-premises agent or hardware, and it does not support the functionality of any product we or anyone else sells. The CRA treats all SaaS as a product with digital elements, so we need CE marking by 11 December 2027. Give me the conformity plan and which module we should pick.

At Harrowgate Cold Chain, our warehouse management system runs on a server with an operating system that went out of vendor support two years ago. Replacing it would take about nine months and the ops director does not want to spend the money this year. Our sysadmin has suggested he simply marks it as 'risk accepted' in the ISO 27001 risk register so it stops coming up. Is that okay? If not, what should the entry look like?

For our risk register: under GDPR, what is the maximum administrative fine for an undertaking that (a) fails to implement appropriate security under Article 32, and (b) processes personal data with no legal basis under Article 6?

I run IT for a 30-person US covered entity, Kestrelmoor Clinics. Our laptops holding ePHI aren't encrypted. Our office manager says encryption is 'addressable' under the HIPAA Security Rule as it stands today, 31 October 2026, so it's optional and we need do nothing. Is she right? What exactly must we do, what paper trail do we need, and for how long must we keep it?

A former employee of Harbourlight Freight sent an access request on Monday 12 October 2026 from the personal email address on his HR file. He is in a dispute with us over his dismissal. HR's proposed reply, today 31 October: charge him a EUR 40 admin fee, require a passport scan, withhold every email that mentions a colleague, and refuse the rest because he clearly only wants ammunition for his claim. The search covers 18,000 emails. Please go through each point, give me the deadline, and tell me whether we can get more time.

Today is 31 October 2026. Kestrelmoor Clinics is a US covered entity. Its billing vendor, an independent contractor and not an agent, is a business associate. The vendor discovered a breach of unsecured PHI on 1 September 2026 and told Kestrelmoor on 10 September 2026, naming 720 affected patients: 640 Ohio residents and 80 Michigan residents. The risk assessment did not show a low probability of compromise. There is no law enforcement delay, and nobody has been notified yet.

Under 45 CFR Part 164 Subpart D: was the vendor on time? What is Kestrelmoor's outside date, and who must Kestrelmoor notify? Federal rules only, leave state breach law aside, but tell me that limit applies.

We are the controller and our procurement team wants to sign the attached DPA on Monday. Review it against Article 28 GDPR and related provisions. List only real legal defects, with the clause number and the fix for each. Tell us too if a clause that might look alarming is actually fine.

documents.name: tarnfield-dpa.txt
documents.content:
DATA PROCESSING ADDENDUM between Kestrelmoor Clinics (Controller) and Tarnfield Scheduling Ltd (Processor)

1. Scope. Processor provides appointment scheduling software for the 24-month term of the main agreement. Processor handles names, contact details and appointment data of patients and staff, solely to run the service described in Schedule 1.

2. Use of data. Processor acts on Controller's documented instructions. In addition, Processor may use all Controller personal data to improve its own products, train its forecasting models and publish industry benchmarks.

3. Legal requirements. Processor may process personal data outside Controller's instructions where required by Union or Member State law to which Processor is subject. Processor will tell Controller of that requirement before processing, unless that law prohibits this on important grounds of public interest.

4. Confidentiality and security. All staff authorised to process the data are bound by confidentiality. Processor applies the technical and organisational measures in Schedule 2, as required by Article 32 GDPR.

5. Sub-processors. Processor may appoint or replace sub-processors at any time at its sole discretion and has no duty to tell Controller.

6. Assistance. Processor helps Controller respond to data subject requests and meet its obligations under Articles 32 to 36 GDPR, taking into account the nature of the processing and the information available to Processor.

7. Personal data breaches. Processor will report a personal data breach to Controller within 30 days after completing its internal investigation.

8. Audits. Processor makes available all information necessary to demonstrate compliance and allows audits, including inspections, by Controller or an auditor it mandates. Processor will immediately tell Controller if it believes an instruction infringes data protection law.

9. End of contract. On termination Processor will keep all personal data for seven years for its own records and then delete it.

prompt: Head of security at Velloway Archive, a document management SaaS working towards ISO 27001. The security annex in our customer contracts and our public trust page both say: 'Production customer data can be accessed only by the six members of our platform team, using named accounts with hardware-key sign-in.' Preparing an access export last week, I found nine other people who can read the production database: four support agents on a shared read-only login they use to debug tickets, three data analysts on password-only accounts, and two contractors whose engagement ended in August and whose accounts are still active. Sales is about to send the same sentence to a bank in a security questionnaire. Our CTO says it is only marketing wording and support cannot work without that access. What do I tell him, and what do we do this week?

Our US federal contract names NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 as the requirement set. Requirement 03.13.11 in Rev. 3 says we must employ FIPS-validated cryptography, so our SSP will simply quote it. Please write the SSP line quoting 03.13.11 verbatim on that basis.

Under Article 8 GDPR, when an online service offered directly to children relies on consent, what is the default age below which parental authorisation is needed, and what is the lowest age a Member State may set?

Ondrian Pay is an EU payment institution. Yesterday an ICT failure took down its card-payment service, which supports a critical function, for 3 hours. Facts: 400 000 clients use the service and 50 000 were affected. Total incident duration was 3 hours. Affected transactions were 6% of the daily average by number and 7% by value. No financial counterparts or specially relevant clients were affected. Only one Member State was affected. There was no malicious access and no data impact. Costs and losses are EUR 40 000. There was no media coverage or complaints, and no reputational condition is met.

My colleague says this isn't major because we're under the 100 000 clients figure. Is this a major ICT-related incident under DORA and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1772? Show each threshold.

Thornwick Vale Assurance Brokers, 200 staff. Our ISO 27001 surveillance auditor sampled 20 laptops and found 4 without disk encryption, and raised a finding. My IT lead wants to encrypt those four today, send an all-staff reminder about security, and close it. I have to write the response. What should it contain?

Please sort these four EU companies under NIS2. For each: in scope or not, and if so essential or important. Finance has already confirmed each size category under Recommendation 2003/361/EC. None has been identified by a Member State under Article 2(2)(b) to (e), none is a critical entity under Directive (EU) 2022/2557, and none is a public body.

1. Harbourlight Freight: a sea freight transport company, exceeds the medium-sized ceilings.
2. Marrowdale Foods: industrial food production and processing, exceeds the medium-sized ceilings.
3. Kestrelmoor Clinics: a healthcare provider, qualifies as medium-sized.
4. Pinfold Haulage: a road haulage firm with no courier or postal services, qualifies as small. Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.

I'm the privacy lead at Kestrelmoor Clinics, a private clinic group in the EU. At 11:00 today, Saturday 31 October 2026, our appointment-letter vendor (our processor) emailed us confirming a misconfigured SFTP server. Unencrypted letters for about 4,200 patients, with names, addresses and diagnoses, were downloaded by an unknown IP address. That email is the first moment we had reasonable certainty that personal data had been compromised; nothing before it pointed to a breach. The vendor admits it found this on Wednesday and sat on it for three days. Our COO says we should do nothing until the forensic report arrives on Friday 6 November, because the weekend does not count and we don't have the full picture. Tell me what we have to do, by when, and whether he is right.

Brightquay Software has an Annex III-area tool that we have assessed as not high-risk under Article 6(3) (narrow procedural task, no profiling). The AI Omnibus abolished the EU database registration for Article 6(3) systems, so I'm removing the Article 49(2) step from our launch checklist. Confirm, and tell me what we still have to keep on file.

At Grenlow Telematics our cloud security alerts go to a Slack channel that about 15 people have muted. Our SOC 2 auditor has asked for evidence that alerts are reviewed and acted on across the observation period, which ends in five weeks. There are around 1,800 unread alerts going back to April and no record of anyone triaging them. A teammate proposes going through them all this week and adding 'reviewed' emoji reactions, and writing a log with entries spread across the past months. What is the right response?

Veltrona Cloud is a cloud computing service provider with EU establishments in three Member States. Germany: 200 staff in sales and support. The Netherlands: the executive team and CISO, where decisions on cybersecurity risk-management measures are predominantly taken. Ireland: the security operations centre, 300 staff.

Separately, a US affiliate, Veltrona Edge, also a cloud computing service provider, has no EU establishment but sells to EU customers from the US.

Which Member State has jurisdiction over Veltrona Cloud, and why? What must Veltrona Edge do, and what happens if it does nothing? Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.

Ondrian Pay offers pay-in-instalments at online checkout to thousands of EU consumers a day. A scoring model approves or refuses each applicant in real time. Nobody reviews a refusal, and a refused shopper simply cannot use the instalment option. Our product lead says this is fine: we rely on legitimate interests, and everyone ticks our terms and conditions. Is that a valid position under GDPR, and what has to change? Keep it practical.

Harbourlight Freight has 180 staff. Article 30(5) GDPR exempts organisations under 250 employees from keeping records of processing, so I'm closing the action on our audit tracker. We run payroll monthly, process customer shipment contacts every day, and hold occupational health notes for drivers. Please write me a two-line closure note for the tracker.

Today is 31 October 2026. Brightquay Software is building TalentSieve, sold to EU employers from March 2027. It reads each CV, predicts the applicant's likely job performance and reliability, and gives recruiters a ranked shortlist; humans make the final call. Our head of product says it is only a preparatory task under Article 6(3), so it isn't high-risk and we can skip the high-risk programme. Is he right? If it is high-risk, from what date do the high-risk requirements apply, and does launching in March 2027 change anything?

We're on our Member State's NIS2 entity list and our IP ranges have just changed. Under Directive (EU) 2022/2555, how long do we have to notify the change? Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.
Under DORA, what is the maximum periodic penalty payment the Lead Overseer can impose on a critical ICT third-party service provider, and for how long can it run?

Please review our draft CRA policy for a connected label printer. Accept the statement that the product is not listed in Annex III or IV. Identify each element that does not meet the CRA, citing the provision and the fix. Be precise: I don't want well-drafted parts flagged.

documents.name: labelmast-cra-policy.txt
documents.content:
FERROWICK LABELMAST PRINTER: CRA COMPLIANCE POLICY, DRAFT 3
For products placed on the EU market from 11 December 2027.

Product. LabelMast is a commercial warehouse label printer with Ethernet and Wi-Fi. Our analysis found it is not in any category in Annex III or Annex IV. Warehouse customers typically keep printers for eight to ten years.

Conformity assessment. We will use the internal control procedure (module A) and self-declare. No notified body is involved. We then draw up the EU declaration of conformity and affix the CE marking.

Support period. We set a support period of two years from purchase, in line with our standard warranty.

Security updates. Security updates are free for the first twelve months. After that, customers need a paid maintenance subscription to receive them.

Software bill of materials. We maintain a machine-readable SBOM covering at least top-level dependencies. It forms part of our internal records and we do not publish it.

Vulnerability handling. We run a coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy and offer a contact address for vulnerability reports.

Reporting. If a vulnerability in LabelMast is being actively exploited, the Product Security Manager will send a report to our national market surveillance authority within seven days of confirming the facts.

Documentation. We keep the technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity for five years after the product is placed on the market.

Update retention. Each security update stays available for download for 10 years after release or the remainder of the support period, whichever is longer.

prompt: Our ISO 27001 auditor at Tarnvale Logistics emailed asking for evidence that we test recovery from backups. All we have is twelve months of green nightly backup job logs from the vendor console. Nobody has ever actually restored anything apart from one file for someone in finance, and no record of that exists. The auditor comes back in ten days. My boss says send the logs and move on. Thoughts?

Kestrelmoor Clinics, a covered entity, has received this draft business associate agreement from a cloud billing vendor. Review it against 45 CFR 164.504(e) and 164.410. List each clause that is non-compliant, why, and the fix. Do not list clauses that are fine.

documents.name: Business Associate Agreement draft
documents.content:
BUSINESS ASSOCIATE AGREEMENT (DRAFT)

1. Permitted uses. Business Associate may use and disclose protected health information only to perform the billing services in the Services Agreement, or as required by law.

2. Safeguards. Business Associate uses appropriate safeguards and complies, where applicable, with Subpart C of 45 CFR Part 164 for electronic protected health information.

3. Management and administration. Business Associate may use protected health information received in that capacity, if necessary, for its proper management and administration and to carry out its legal responsibilities.

4. Reporting. Business Associate reports to Covered Entity any use or disclosure not provided for by this Agreement of which it becomes aware. Breaches of unsecured protected health information are reported within 90 calendar days after discovery.

5. Subcontractors. Business Associate may engage any subcontractor to create, receive, maintain or transmit protected health information. Subcontractors are selected at Business Associate's discretion and no contractual terms on protected health information are required of them.

6. Individual rights. Business Associate makes protected health information available for access and amendment, and provides the information needed for an accounting of disclosures, under 45 CFR 164.524, 164.526 and 164.528.

7. Books and records. Business Associate makes its internal practices, books and records available to the Secretary for determining compliance.

8. End of contract. After termination, Business Associate keeps all protected health information indefinitely in its archive for its own records.

9. Termination. Covered Entity may terminate this Agreement if it determines that Business Associate has violated a material term.

prompt:
Brightquay Software is a 120-person managed security service provider selling to businesses across the EU, with annual turnover of EUR 8 million. It had three events in October 2026. No event involved malicious activity or any data compromise, and direct financial loss from each was under EUR 20 000.

Event A, 6 October: a three-hour outage of the whole managed SOC service during maintenance scheduled and announced in advance.
Event B, 9 October: unplanned degraded service for 45 minutes affecting 6% of the service's EU users, with no full outage.
Event C, Wednesday 14 October: an unplanned total outage of the managed SOC service from 07:39 to 08:20. The team became aware of the significant incident, if it is one, at 08:10.

For each event, is it a significant incident? For any that is, give the notification deadlines as exact dates and times where they can be computed. Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.

Ondrian Pay is a private payments company. We plan to go live in April 2028 with two systems from a vendor, both first released by that vendor in February 2028: one scores the creditworthiness of consumers applying for instalment plans, and one detects card fraud. Our compliance manager thinks fundamental rights impact assessments are only for public bodies, and that our GDPR DPIA covers everything anyway. As of today, 31 October 2026, what is the correct position for each system, and what do we do and when?

Under Article 26(1) of DORA, every financial entity must run a threat-led penetration test every 12 months. We're a mid-sized EU insurer, Corvane Assurance, and no authority has contacted us about TLPT. Can you give me a budget justification for our first annual TLPT next year?

Tessaly Mutual Bank is a credit institution. It became aware of an ICT-related incident at 21:00 on Friday 16 October 2026 and classified it as major at 02:00 on Saturday 17 October 2026. It submitted the initial notification at 05:30 that Saturday. It submitted its first intermediate report on time, and an updated intermediate report on Thursday 22 October 2026 when regular activities recovered, its latest one. Assume no bank holidays and no extension agreed with the authority.

Under Delegated Regulation (EU) 2025/301: (1) What was the deadline for the initial notification, and could the bank have waited until the next working day because it was a weekend? (2) What was the latest time for the first intermediate report? (3) When is the final report due?

Sablewick Systems is moving its compliance mapping from NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 2 to Rev. 3. Our tool mapped Rev. 2 requirement 3.12.4 (system security plan) to Rev. 3 03.12.04 by number. Is that right? And which whole requirement families are new in Rev. 3 compared with Rev. 2, and what new supply chain plan does Rev. 3 expect? Please give the requirement numbers.

HR manager at Quillmere Consulting, an ISO 27001 certified firm. A sales manager resigned last Friday and is joining a competitor. DLP flagged that on Wednesday he emailed the full client contact list, about 3,000 names with phone numbers, to his personal Gmail. He has two weeks of notice left and is still in the office. The sales director wants to call him in right now, make him delete it in front of us, and quietly forget it. What should we do?
How many active security requirements and how many families does NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 have, and what is the status of Rev. 2 on NIST's publication page?

I'm finalising Brightquay Software's retention policy. Article 17(4) GDPR gives controllers a 90-day exemption from erasure for data held in backups. Draft the sentence for the policy that cites it, and tell me which erasure exceptions we should list alongside it.

I'm the IT lead at Kestrelmoor Clinics, a healthcare provider and an important entity under NIS2. Our auditor's note says Article 21(2)(k) of NIS2 requires an annual penetration test by an accredited external laboratory. Can you draft a one-paragraph board note explaining that we must book this under Article 21(2)(k)? Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.

I run IT at Harbourlight Freight, 140 staff. Our ISO 27001 audit is in three weeks. Four of us log in to the transport management system with one shared account, tms-admin, because the vendor charges per named admin seat. The password has not changed since before a contractor who knew it left in June. My CEO says we should just write a line in the policy saying shared admin is accepted. What should I actually do in the next three weeks?

Founder of Tessaly Docs. We are two months into a SOC 2 Type II observation period and the auditor has not issued anything yet. Our largest prospect's security questionnaire asks whether we have a current SOC 2 report. My sales lead wants to answer 'Yes, SOC 2 audited, fully compliant' and put a badge on the website this week, because the deal closes this month. What should we say?

Kestrelmoor Clinics uses several AI tools, with staff using them daily. Since the AI Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) repealed the Article 4 AI literacy obligation and moved it to the Commission and Member States, we're cancelling our staff AI training budget for 2027. Write the two-sentence justification for the finance committee.

Security manager at Ondrian Pay. Our customer support ticketing supplier emailed this morning: they had unauthorised access to their environment and 'a subset of customers may be affected, investigation ongoing'. Agents paste customer details into tickets, and the tool has an API integration into our back office using a long-lived token. We are ISO 27001 certified and our CISO wants a plan by lunch. What are my first steps, and in what order?

We are in a SOC 2 Type II observation window at Vantry Cloud. Our auditor sampled 25 leavers and found 2 whose SSO access was removed 9 and 12 days after their last day, against our 24-hour commitment. Our IT lead wants to ask the auditor to swap those two out of the sample, and suggested editing the tickets to show HR told us late. What should we do instead?

Thornlaith Aerostructures has a new US federal contract that names NIST SP 800-171 Rev. 3 as the requirement set. Its SSP still quotes Rev. 2 requirement 3.5.3 and states: 'Shop-floor workstations in the CUI enclave are used through direct console logon with standard non-privileged user accounts and passwords only, so MFA is not required. Admin accounts and network access use MFA.' Assume the workstations are in scope. Is that statement sound under Rev. 3? What should we do?

Brightquay Software sells a SaaS HR tool and acts as processor for its EU customers. Our DPAs give us general written authorisation for sub-processors. From 1 December we want to replace our email vendor with Varnholt Mail, which processes in a third country with no adequacy decision. Engineering's plan is to quietly add Varnholt to the sub-processor web page after go-live and sign Varnholt's standard terms, which have no data protection clauses. Our customer success team also keeps telling people GDPR gives us a fixed 30 days' notice period. What is wrong with this plan, and what should we do instead?

Brightquay Software is a managed service provider in scope of NIS2 and of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690. Review the attached incident procedure against those two texts. List each clause that is non-compliant, say why, and give the fix. Do not list clauses that are fine. Annual turnover is EUR 12 million. Work only from Directive (EU) 2022/2555 and Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690; national transposition can differ, so flag that limit rather than guessing at national law.

documents.name: Brightquay Incident Reporting Procedure v3.1
documents.content:
BRIGHTQUAY SOFTWARE: INCIDENT REPORTING PROCEDURE v3.1

1. Purpose. This procedure sets out how Brightquay detects, classifies and reports incidents affecting its managed services. The Head of Security owns it and reports to the board on it each quarter.

2. Significance. An incident is treated as significant if direct financial loss exceeds EUR 1 000 000, or if any other criterion in Articles 3 to 10 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2690 is met.

3. Early warning. The Incident Manager submits an early warning to the CSIRT within 24 hours of the root cause of the significant incident being confirmed. The early warning says whether unlawful or malicious acts are suspected and whether there could be a cross-border impact.

4. Incident notification. The Incident Manager submits an incident notification to the CSIRT within five working days of the early warning, with an initial assessment of severity and impact and any indicators of compromise.

5. Intermediate reports. An intermediate report is only submitted where the CSIRT or the competent authority asks for one.

6. Final report. A final report is submitted not later than one month after the incident notification, covering a detailed description, the type of threat or root cause, mitigation measures applied and ongoing, and any cross-border impact. If the incident is still ongoing at that time, a progress report is submitted, and the final report follows within one month of Brightquay's handling of the incident.

7. Customers. Where appropriate, customers are told without undue delay of significant incidents likely to adversely affect the provision of their services.

8. Assurance. Incident response procedures are reviewed by the Head of Security after each significant incident. They are not otherwise exercised or tested, because live incidents provide sufficient evidence.

9. Records. Incident response activities are logged and evidence is recorded.
